questions.text: How does the compression-release principle operate in promenade architecturlea?

options.text: All spaces should be uniformly proportioned to avoid confusing occupants, ensuring a consistent spatial experience
Compression refers to HVAC systems; release refers to ventilation—unrelated to spatial experience, focusing instead on mechanical systems
Narrow, low spaces compress; tall, wide spaces release, creating psychological rhythm and emotional impact through alternation
Compression occurs at entrances; release occurs at exits, providing a clear transition between different spatial zones

rationale.a: Variation creates interest; uniformity creates monotony.
rationale.b: Compression-release is a spatial and psychological principle, not mechanical systems.
rationale.d: Compression-release can occur throughout a building's sequence, not just at entry and exit.
rationale.correct: Compression-release contrasts narrow/low (compression) with tall/wide (release), creating emotional rhythm and engagement through spatial variation.
rationale.takeaway: Compression-release contrasts narrow/low (compression) with tall/wide (release), creating emotional rhythm and engagement through spatial variation.

questions.text: Why is consistency of riser and tread heights maintained within a 5 mm tolerance on a single stair flight?

options.text: To match aesthetic preferences of architects and building designers, ensuring a visually pleasing and uniform appearance
To permit the body's muscle memory to establish rhythm; inconsistency disrupts this rhythm and creates trip hazards
To simplify construction and reduce building cost by minimizing material waste and labor time
To ensure structural integrity of the stair system, preventing potential failures due to uneven load distribution

rationale.a: Aesthetic preference is secondary to safety.
rationale.c: While cost is a factor, safety is the primary reason.
rationale.d: Structural integrity is separate from step‑to‑step consistency.
rationale.correct: Muscle memory expects identical step dimensions; variations beyond the allowable tolerance (5 mm per PD 1096) cause stumbling and falls.
rationale.takeaway: Muscle memory expects identical step dimensions; variations beyond the allowable tolerance (5 mm per PD 1096) cause stumbling and falls.

questions.text: Using the 2R+T proportional rule, if a stair has a 170 mm riser, what tread depth is most comfortable?

rationale.b: 2(170) + 300 = 640 mm, at the upper limit but acceptable.
rationale.correct: Using 2(170) + T = 600–630 mm: 340 + 270 = 610 mm, within the comfortable range. 270 mm is also ≥ the 250 mm minimum required by PD 1096.
rationale.takeaway: 270 mm is also ≥ the 250 mm minimum required by PD 1096.

questions.text: A residential corridor must accommodate single-file passage with minimal design constraints. What is the minimum required width under PD 1096?

rationale.b: 1200 mm is required for two-way traffic or corridors serving more than one dwelling unit, not for single-file passage.
rationale.c: 750 mm violates the code and creates accessibility barriers.
rationale.d: 1500 mm exceeds requirements and is not necessary for single-file movement.
rationale.correct: PD 1096 Rule VIII Sec. 804 requires a minimum clear width of 900 mm for residential corridors; this permits single-file passage.
rationale.takeaway: 804 requires a minimum clear width of 900 mm for residential corridors; this permits single-file passage.

questions.text: Why do level changes of 300–600 mm between spaces create stronger territorial separation than smaller steps?

options.text: Because large steps are easier to climb and therefore more noticeable, enhancing spatial awareness
Because the body must pause and consciously navigate the change, forcing acknowledgment of spatial boundary
Because building codes require greater separation for safety purposes, ensuring compliance with regulations
Because large steps create more dramatic shadows and visual contrast, emphasizing the division

rationale.a: Larger steps are harder, not easier, to climb.
rationale.c: Codes regulate accessibility, but territorial separation is psychological and experiential.
rationale.d: Visual contrast may contribute, but the kinesthetic response is primary.
rationale.correct: A change of 300–600 mm requires deliberate navigation; the body cannot pass without attention, creating psychological and kinesthetic acknowledgment of a boundary.
rationale.takeaway: A change of 300–600 mm requires deliberate navigation; the body cannot pass without attention, creating psychological and kinesthetic acknowledgment of a boundary.

questions.text: A residential building's main circulation corridor should accommodate two-way traffic comfortably. What is the minimum width under PD 1096?

rationale.a: 900 mm accommodates single-file only; two people must synchronize.
rationale.b: 800 mm forces collision; two people cannot pass comfortably.
rationale.c: 1500 mm exceeds the requirement and may waste circulation space.
rationale.correct: For corridors serving more than one dwelling unit or forming part of the main circulation, PD 1096 generally requires a minimum width of 1200 mm to allow two people to pass comfortably.
rationale.takeaway: For corridors serving more than one dwelling unit or forming part of the main circulation, PD 1096 generally requires a minimum width of 1200 mm to allow two people to pass comfortably.

questions.text: Le Corbusier's term for the carefully choreographed sequence of spaces and experiences as one moves through a building is:

options.text: Kinesthetic rhythm, which refers to the movement and flow of spaces in a dynamic manner
Circulation sequence, emphasizing the planned path and movement through architectural spaces
Spatial composition, focusing on the arrangement and organization of spaces within a structure

rationale.b: Kinesthetic rhythm is a general term but not Le Corbusier's nomenclature.
rationale.c: Circulation sequence is functional; promenade architecturale emphasizes aesthetic intent.
rationale.d: Spatial composition is too broad and lacks the movement emphasis.
rationale.correct: Promenade architecturale' (architectural promenade) is Le Corbusier's specific term for intentional spatial sequences experienced through movement.
rationale.takeaway: Promenade architecturale' (architectural promenade) is Le Corbusier's specific term for intentional spatial sequences experienced through movement.

questions.text: The minimum tread depth for residential stairs according to PD 1096 is:

rationale.a: 200–220 mm is below the minimum and creates unsafe foot positioning.
rationale.c: 350–400 mm exceeds comfortable depth and leads to disproportionately long stair runs.
rationale.d: 150–180 mm is riser height, not tread depth.
rationale.correct: PD 1096 Rule VIII Sec. 806(b) requires a minimum tread depth of 250 mm; a comfortable tread depth is typically 250–300 mm, ensuring foot stability.
rationale.takeaway: 806(b) requires a minimum tread depth of 250 mm; a comfortable tread depth is typically 250–300 mm, ensuring foot stability.

questions.text: An accessible ramp must span a 1.5‑meter vertical height. According to BP 344 (2024 Revised IRR), what is the minimum horizontal length required at the maximum allowable slope?

rationale.a: 15 m would correspond to a 1:10 slope, which is too steep for an accessible building ramp.
rationale.b: 20 m would correspond to a 1:13.3 slope, steeper than permitted.
rationale.c: 25 m would correspond to a 1:16.7 slope, still steeper than 1:20.
rationale.correct: BP 344 2024 Revised IRR Section 5.2.2 requires a maximum slope of 1:20 for accessible ramps in buildings. For a 1.5 m rise, the minimum horizontal run is 1.5 × 20 = 30 m.
rationale.takeaway: For a 1.5 m rise, the minimum horizontal run is 1.5 × 20 = 30 m.

questions.text: The maximum accessible ramp slope for buildings according to BP 344 (2024 Revised IRR) is:

rationale.a: 1:8 is far too steep and would be unsafe for wheelchair users.
rationale.b: 1:10 exceeds the allowable slope under Philippine accessibility law.
rationale.c: 1:15 is still steeper than 1:20 and is not compliant.
rationale.correct: BP 344 2024 Revised IRR Section 5.2.2 mandates a maximum slope of 1:20 for accessible ramps within buildings. Slopes steeper than 1:20 are not permitted for building ramps; the 1:12 slope is only allowed for curb ramps or very short exterior ramps.
rationale.takeaway: Slopes steeper than 1:20 are not permitted for building ramps; the 1:12 slope is only allowed for curb ramps or very short exterior ramps.

questions.text: Kinesthetics in architecture is best defined as:

options.text: The study of the body in motion through space, including the aesthetic and psychological experience of moving through a building
The scientific measurement of standing and seated human postures, which is crucial for ergonomic design
The principles governing accessible design for people with mobility disabilities, ensuring compliance with accessibility standards
The analysis of how light changes as occupants move through spaces, affecting visual comfort and spatial perception

rationale.c: This describes accessibility, related but distinct from kinesthetics.
rationale.d: This describes dynamic light perception, not kinesthetics.
rationale.correct: Kinesthetics studies how architecture is experienced through the body in motion—stairs, corridors, transitions—and their psychological impact.
rationale.takeaway: Kinesthetics studies how architecture is experienced through the body in motion—stairs, corridors, transitions—and their psychological impact.

questions.text: According to the National Building Code (PD 1096), the maximum riser height for residential stairs is:

rationale.a: 250–280 mm exceeds the legal maximum and is also the typical tread depth range.
rationale.c: 100–120 mm is below the minimum and would cause inefficient overstriding.
rationale.d: 150–180 mm is a comfort range, but the maximum allowable under Philippine law is 200 mm.
rationale.correct: PD 1096 Rule VIII Sec. 806(b) allows a maximum riser height of 200 mm for residential stairs and 190 mm for commercial; a range of 200–220 mm is the practical maximum, though comfort is best between 150–180 mm.
rationale.takeaway: 806(b) allows a maximum riser height of 200 mm for residential stairs and 190 mm for commercial; a range of 200–220 mm is the practical maximum, though comfort is best between 150–180 mm.

questions.text: In designing a building entrance threshold, a 15–20 mm step height signals to occupants that:

options.text: Wheelchair access is available through this entrance
A transition or boundary between spaces is occurring
The building is not accessible and separate accessible entry is elsewhere
Construction has failed and a safety hazard exists

rationale.a: Accessible entrances must have a level threshold (≤6 mm vertical change) or a ramp.
rationale.c: The step signals transition, but it does not by itself indicate whether an accessible entry exists elsewhere.
rationale.d: 15–20 mm is an intentional design element, not a construction failure.
rationale.correct: A 15–20 mm step is perceptible as a boundary. However, under BP 344, any vertical change greater than 13 mm requires a ramp or beveled treatment to be accessible.
rationale.takeaway: However, under BP 344, any vertical change greater than 13 mm requires a ramp or beveled treatment to be accessible.
